title: The Catechism (1992)
hook: a single summary of Catholic belief, written for the whole world

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hard day: the abuse crisis, and the word safeguarding. Your line was survivors first. Did you find out how a concern would be reported where you belong? Day nine hundred thirty.

If someone asked you, what do Catholics actually believe, where would you send them? A priest, maybe. A website. A grandmother. For a long time the answer depended on where you lived: each country, sometimes each diocese, had its own little question-and-answer book. Children memorized them. Who made us? God made us. There had been a catechism for the whole Church once before, written after the Council of Trent for parish priests. Then the bishops of the world, meeting in Rome, asked for a new one: one book, for the whole Church, that set out the faith in order. It took years of drafting, and the bishops were asked for their comments. The result is a thick book with numbered paragraphs, sitting today on parish shelves and on phones. It's called the Catechism of the Catholic Church.
screen: `WHAT DO CATHOLICS BELIEVE?` → `A LITTLE BOOK FOR EACH PLACE.` → `ONE BOOK FOR THE WHOLE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Open the book and its plan is plain. First, the shape. The Catechism is built in four parts, and once you know them the whole book opens up. The faith professed: the Creed, line by line. The faith celebrated: the liturgy and the sacraments. The faith lived: the life in Christ, including the Ten Commandments. And the faith prayed: prayer, ending with the Our Father, line by line. What Catholics believe, how they worship, how they live, and how they pray. Second, the numbers. Every paragraph has a number, and the book cross-references itself in the margins, so one paragraph about baptism points you to others about grace, about the Church, about water at Easter. People cite it by number, the way you'd cite a verse. Third, who it's for. John Paul the Second, in the document that introduced it, called it a sure norm for teaching the faith, meant first for bishops and teachers, and then for anyone who wants to know what the Church believes. It was never meant to replace local catechisms, but to be the reference they draw on. Fourth, the sources. Open it almost anywhere and the paragraphs are stitched from scripture, from the councils, from saints and early writers. Luke opens his Gospel by telling Theophilus why he wrote it, in the Douay-Rheims: "That thou mayest know the verity of those words in which thou hast been instructed." The Catechism sets out to do the same thing at the size of a whole Church: one summary, in order, so the faith can be known, not just guessed at.
screen: `FOUR PARTS: BELIEVE, WORSHIP, LIVE, PRAY.` · `NUMBERED PARAGRAPHS, CITED LIKE VERSES.` · `A SURE NORM FOR TEACHING.` · `STITCHED FROM SCRIPTURE AND SAINTS.` · then, large: `THAT THOU MAYEST KNOW THE VERITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to read one paragraph. Settle, and breathe. Of the four parts, believe, worship, live, pray, which one are you most curious about right now? Don't pick the one you think you should. Pick the one with a question in it. Then name the question, in a few words, to yourself. What is grace? Why confession? What does the Church say about work? Hold that question gently, without trying to answer it yet. If you pray, you can ask for understanding. If you don't, just stay curious. The bell holds the time.
The Catechism. The Catechism of the Catholic Church: one summary of the faith, in four parts, in numbered paragraphs, for the whole Church.
Your line: one summary. Today, find the part of the Catechism that holds your question, and read one paragraph. Just one, slowly. Day nine hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Catholics use the Catechism of the Catholic Church as a reference in parish classes, adult formation and preparation for the sacraments, often citing it by paragraph number; shorter local catechisms and the Compendium draw on it.

notes: Claims rule: no date spoken; 'it took years of drafting, and many bishops sent in corrections' is a general claim about the drafting process (Fidei Depositum describes the consultation of bishops); confirm or soften.
That the request came from the bishops meeting in Rome (the Extraordinary Synod) is from Fidei Depositum; confirm.
Fidei Depositum: confirm 'sure norm for teaching the faith' and that it is addressed first to bishops, and that it is not meant to replace local catechisms.
The 'Who made me? God made me' line is from the Baltimore / Penny Catechism tradition, offered as an example; confirm acceptable.
Editor: replaced 'many bishops sent in corrections' with the consultation of bishops; varied the teach opener.

Auditor (serious): the hook called a catechism for the whole Church 'something new'; the Roman Catechism after Trent was a precedent (Fidei Depositum itself cites it), now said. The memorized line was misquoted ('Who made me? God made me'); now the Baltimore Catechism's 'Who made us? God made us' (the Penny Catechism has 'Who made you? God made me'); confirm wording.
